extracted.intended_audience: researchers reporting multivariable prediction model studies; peer reviewers and journal editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing clear, informative journal and conference abstracts for multivariable diagnostic or prognostic prediction model studies (development, external validation, added value, or updating), including required items and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title — identification of study type, target population, and outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of the study as developing, validating, or updating a prediction model; the target population; and the outcome to be predicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An informative title requires the following 4 aspects: the term “prediction model” or a synonym, the type of prediction model study (development, external validation, added value, model updating, or a combination), the target population, and the outcome to be predicted. (Example: 'Development and validation of a model to predict the risk of exacerbations in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Background — healthcare context and rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: A brief explanation of the health care context (including whether diagnostic or prognostic) and rationale for developing, validating, or updating the model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain the intended use and clinical context so readers understand the intended application of the model and why it was needed. (Example provided describing why identifying endocarditis in febrile injection drug users is clinically important.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives — study aims and whether development/validation/updating
rubrics_metrics.description: Study objectives, including whether the study describes the development, validation, or updating of a model. For validation of an existing model, give the name or describe the model being validated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives should clearly state the study type (development, validation, updating). If validating an existing model, include the model name or a description to facilitate identification. (Reported clearly in 76% of reviewed publications.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods — study design or source of data
rubrics_metrics.description: Study design or source of data (for example, cohort, registry, routine care data, or randomized trial), separately for the development and validation data sets, if applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporting data source and design helps assess applicability and risk of bias; differences between development and validation datasets should be stated separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods — participant eligibility and setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Participant eligibility criteria and setting where the data were collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide eligibility criteria and setting to inform generalizability (example: description of Women's Health Study cohort). (Reported in many but not all reviewed abstracts.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods — outcome definition and prediction horizon
rubrics_metrics.description: Outcome to be predicted by the model, including time horizon of predictions in case of prognostic models (for example, 3-year overall survival).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify the exact outcome and prediction horizon because predictive ability depends on these. (Example: 'The outcome was 5-year all-cause mortality.')

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods — statistical model/algorithm and internal validation approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical model or algorithm used (for example, logistic regression, Cox regression, random forest, or neural network) and approach for internal validation (for development studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State which model/algorithm was used and, for development/updating studies, how internal validation was performed (e.g., bootstrap resampling, split-sample, cross-validation). Internal validation is important to assess overfitting and optimism; reporting it in the abstract helps judge risk of bias. Examples include traditional regression and machine-learning approaches; mention training and validation dataset sizes if relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Results — number of participants and outcome events
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of participants and outcome events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report total sample size and number of events, because these determine precision and risk of bias in performance estimates. If sample size or event counts are small, that increases risk of biased performance estimates. (Overall sample size reported commonly; number with outcome reported less often.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Results — predictors in the final model (development studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Predictors in the final model (for development studies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List predictors included in the final model; if too numerous for an abstract, describe predictor categories (for example, sociodemographic, history/examination items, laboratory tests, disease characteristics). (Reported for 63% of development studies.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Results — performance measures (at least calibration and discrimination) and added-value/updating results
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance measures, at least calibration and discrimination (with confidence intervals), and results for added value of predictors or for model updating, if applicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include key performance metrics — at minimum calibration and discrimination with CIs (preferably optimism-corrected measures). Quantify calibration (eg, calibration slope, calibration in the large) where possible; discrimination often via AUC/C-statistic. Report results of added predictors or model updating (eg, change in c-statistic). Where allowed (conference abstracts), graphical displays can be used. Examples and numeric results are shown. (Discrimination reported more often than calibration in reviewed abstracts.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion/Conclusions — overall interpretation, limitations, and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall interpretation of the results, including implications for practice or research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a brief concluding statement of the main findings, limitations, and implications so readers can judge applicability. (Main conclusions reported in 91% of assessed models.) Example statements note possible overestimation due to treatment or implications for use in primary care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration — registry number and repository name
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration number and name of registry or repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a protocol, trial registration, or data repository exists, provide the registry name and registration number to indicate availability of protocol or data. Although registration of prediction model studies is uncommon, reporting it is helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and applicability of checklist
rubrics_metrics.description: TRIPOD for Abstracts is a checklist of 12 items considered essential for inclusion in all abstracts of prediction model studies; it applies to development, external validation, added value, and model updating studies, across all clinical domains and statistical approaches (including artificial intelligence and machine-learning).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the single checklist for all types of prediction model studies and domains. The checklist items follow the usual abstract structure (Title, Background, Objectives, Methods, Results, Discussion) with an additional Registration item. Consult TRIPOD explanation and elaboration documents for more detail and examples (supplements referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum completeness and abstract length guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The 12 checklist items are the minimum set of information required for informative abstracts about prediction model studies; authors should aim to include them despite word limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although space is limited, the authors believe essential information can be provided in 250–350 words, and the checklist should be treated as the minimum. Editors and peer reviewers can use these items to check abstracts and prevent publication of poorly reported studies. Examples of adequate abstracts are provided in the supplement.
